trump-01.name: I · Le Bateleur
trump-01.Scene: Le Bateleur is reimagined as a satirical carnival scene — the conjurer wears ass's ears, and animals or comic figures crowd the composition alongside the standard table of cups-and-balls paraphernalia. The Paris card turns the lone tradesman of the Marseille tradition into a collective scene of mockery and play, embedding the magician within a social comedy rather than staging him in solitary dexterity.

trump-02.name: II · La Papesse
trump-02.Scene: The Papesse makes a pointedly aversive gesture — an editorial flourish unique to this deck, as if the spiritual woman turns her face or hand away from the viewer with deliberate refusal. Where the Marseille Papesse reads calmly from a book, the Paris figure expresses active rejection, making her secret knowledge feel not merely hidden but withheld.

trump-03.name: III · L'Impératrice
trump-03.Scene: L'Impératrice appears as an enthroned empress in the conventional Italian-suited French tarot manner — eagle shield, sceptre, and crown. The Paris version is broadly comparable to other early French Marseille-tradition cards, the imperial woman seated in authority. The specific staging of this particular card was not separately distinguished in early sources, placing it within the shared visual grammar of 17th-century Parisian tarots.

trump-04.name: IIII · L'Empereur
trump-04.Scene: The Empereur appears head-to-foot in full military armour rather than the robe-and-orb of the Marseille tradition. Where other decks seat the Emperor in courtly regalia, the Paris version militarises him completely — a figure not of civic governance but of armed command, the emperor as soldier rather than sovereign.

trump-05.name: V · Le Pape
trump-05.Scene: Le Pape sits enthroned between two pillars in the standard Marseille manner, blessing two kneeling petitioners. The Paris anonymous version is broadly comparable to the common Marseille type — the papal tiara, the raised hand of benediction, the hierarchical arrangement of pope above acolytes — without the specific iconographic departures that mark other cards in this deck.

trump-06.name: VI · L'Amoureux
trump-06.Scene: L'Amoureux shows a pair of figures under a shooting Cupid, but the elder figure present in the standard Marseille three-person 'choice' composition has been removed. The Paris card reduces the Lovers to a dyad — two figures and Cupid — stripping out the triangular tension of the morality-choice scene and suggesting encounter or mutual attraction rather than a forced decision.

trump-07.name: VII · Le Chariot
trump-07.Scene: Le Chariot is drawn by a goose rather than horses, with a child riding in the car rather than the crowned triumphator of the Marseille tradition. This is one of the deck's most famous and peculiar departures — the chariot of triumph reduced to a farmyard comedy, the child-and-goose substituting for the warrior-and-steeds in a scene that inverts conventional triumph entirely.

trump-08.name: VIII · La Justice
trump-08.Scene: La Justice bears a double or Janus-like face — two faces looking in opposite directions on a single head. This is unique to the Paris anonymous deck and transforms Justice from the single-faced weigher-of-evidence into a figure who simultaneously looks both ways, suggesting not impartiality but the doubled vision of a deity who sees past and future, accuser and accused.

trump-09.name: VIIII · L'Hermite
trump-09.Scene: L'Hermite is broadly comparable to the standard Marseille figure — a bearded man with lantern and staff, withdrawn from the world. The Paris version is noted for a garbled or damaged caption, making the written identification of the card unreliable while the image itself remains within the expected hermit iconography. The solitary elder with his lantern marks the card as a retreat from engagement.

trump-10.name: X · La Roue de Fortune
trump-10.Scene: La Roue de Fortune shows the standard rotating wheel with figures ascending and descending on its rim, a crowned figure at the top and fallen ones at the sides. The Paris card is broadly comparable to the Marseille type — the mechanical wheel as a figure of Fortune's indifference. Specific details of the Paris version await fuller analysis of the original scan.

trump-11.name: XI · La Force
trump-11.Scene: La Force shows a figure subduing a lion — the standard Marseille scene of human mastery over bestial instinct. The Paris card is unremarkable relative to the deck's wilder departures, presenting the woman opening the lion's mouth or restraining the animal in the conventional way. Force here is quiet virtue within an otherwise turbulent deck.

trump-12.name: XII · Le Pendu
trump-12.Scene: Le Pendu shows the inverted hanging figure of the Marseille tradition — a man suspended upside-down from a gallows or scaffold, his legs forming an inverted cross. The Paris card is comparable to the standard type without the exotic departures seen elsewhere in the deck. The Hanged Man's enforced reversal suggests patience, suspension, and the altered perspective of one who sees the world from a position of powerlessness.

trump-13.name: XIII · La Mort
trump-13.Scene: La Mort shows Death's skeleton with scythe harvesting the field of the living, but the Paris card omits the royal and papal heads that appear among the severed parts in the standard Marseille composition. The absence of crowns and mitres from the field of the dead removes Death's traditional claim to equality — kings and popes are no longer explicitly shown as subject to the common harvest.

trump-14.name: XIIII · Tempérance
trump-14.Scene: Tempérance shows an angelic or female figure pouring liquid between two vessels — the standard Marseille image of moderation and temperance. The Paris card is noted for a garbled or damaged caption, a textual peculiarity it shares with the Hermit. The visual content of temperate pouring remains legible even where the written identification has been worn or misprinted.

trump-15.name: XV · Le Diable
trump-15.Scene: Le Diable stands as the card most in need of direct examination in the Paris anonymous deck — the specific iconography of the Parisian devil scene is uncertain, and early sources did not resolve whether it follows the Marseille pedestal-and-bound-imps type or diverges. The card awaits fuller analysis. What is established is the presence of a devil figure in a scene that may carry the deck's satirical energy into its most demonic register.

trump-16.name: XVI · La Maison-Dieu
trump-16.Scene: La Maison-Dieu (the Tower) shows the celestial blow — lightning or divine force striking a tower or structure and sending figures falling. The Paris card belongs to the early French tarot tradition where the Maison-Dieu presents catastrophic rupture as cosmological event. The specific form of the falling structure and the number and type of figures ejected follows the 17th-century Parisian woodcut conventions that shaped this deck's production.

trump-17.name: XVII · L'Étoile
trump-17.Scene: L'Étoile replaces the conventional nude woman pouring water beneath stars with a male scholar measuring or contemplating the heavens — an astronomer or natural philosopher in an interior or observational setting. This is one of the Paris deck's most celebrated departures, transforming a scene of devotional openness into one of scientific inquiry, the star as object of study rather than source of grace.

trump-18.name: XVIII · La Lune
trump-18.Scene: La Lune shows a romantic serenade — a figure beneath the moon making music or performing an amorous gesture for another. Where the Marseille Moon deploys towers, dogs, and a crayfish in a pool of water, the Paris card offers an entirely human domestic scene of courtship under moonlight, associating the moon not with danger and night-dread but with the emotions of love and longing.

trump-19.name: XVIIII · Le Soleil
trump-19.Scene: Le Soleil shows a vanity scene with a mirror and a monkey — a woman admiring herself in a mirror while a monkey watches, in place of the Marseille children beneath a rayed sun. The Paris Sun is one of the most iconographically divergent cards in the deck, replacing solar joy and childhood innocence with the moral emblem of vanitas and simian imitation.

trump-20.name: XX · Le Jugement
trump-20.Scene: Le Jugement shows the angel of resurrection — a winged figure with trumpet above the rising dead — in a composition broadly comparable to the Marseille tradition. Figures emerge from coffins or graves in response to the heavenly summons. The Paris card's specific staging follows the standard eschatological scene without the unusual departures found elsewhere in the deck.

trump-21.name: XXI · Le Monde
trump-21.Scene: Le Monde shows a central haloed figure within a mandorla or oval, flanked by the four evangelist beasts at the corners — the older iconographic type that predates the Marseille dancer-in-wreath convention. The Paris card's four-beast framing places it within the medieval mandorla tradition, associating the World with Christ in glory or the completed cosmos rather than with the dancing anima mundi of later Marseille decks.

deniers-22.name: As de Deniers
deniers-22.Scene: The Roi de Deniers is the King of Coins in the Italian-suited Paris anonymous tarot. He appears enthroned with the large coin or denier as his suit emblem, the conventional seated king of the Italian pip-card tradition. The Paris court figures follow the standard Marseille-derived conventions for the coin suit's highest court rank.

deniers-23.name: Deux de Deniers
deniers-23.Scene: The Reine de Deniers appears as the enthroned Queen of Coins. She holds or displays the coin emblem in the conventional seated-queen posture of the Italian-suited French tarot tradition. The Paris anonymous queen of coins follows the standard Marseille-derived iconography for the suit's feminine court rank.

deniers-24.name: Trois de Deniers
deniers-24.Scene: The Cavalier de Deniers appears as a mounted knight with the coin emblem — a horseman displaying the suit's round disc in the conventional posture of the Italian-suited cavalier card. The mounted position distinguishes the cavalier from the standing valet in the Paris anonymous deck's Italian-tradition court hierarchy.

deniers-25.name: Quatre de Deniers
deniers-25.Scene: The Valet de Deniers is the page or jack of coins — a standing young figure holding or presenting the coin emblem. In the Italian-suited tradition this figure is the lowest of the four court ranks, a youth whose standing posture contrasts with the mounted cavalier and the enthroned senior courts above him.

deniers-26.name: Cinq de Deniers
deniers-26.Scene: The Dix de Deniers shows ten coin emblems distributed across the card in the conventional Italian pip arrangement. In the Paris anonymous tarot the coin pip cards follow the standard symmetrical distribution typical of 17th-century Italian-suited French playing cards, the circular coin shapes arranged in two-column or stacked formations.

deniers-27.name: Six de Deniers
deniers-27.Scene: The Neuf de Deniers shows nine coins in their conventional pip arrangement. The nine-coin card approaches but does not reach the completeness of the ten, the nine circular emblems arranged in the standard Italian pip convention of the Paris anonymous tarot.

deniers-28.name: Sept de Deniers
deniers-28.Scene: The Huit de Deniers shows eight coins in a symmetrical pip arrangement. The eight-coin card has the geometric balance characteristic of even-number pip cards in the Italian-suited tradition, two columns of four or two rows of four evoking the stability of even distribution.

deniers-29.name: Huit de Deniers
deniers-29.Scene: The Sept de Deniers shows seven coins in the conventional pip arrangement. The odd number gives this card a slight visual asymmetry — one coin must sit off-center or alone — and in the Italian pip tradition the seven often places one coin above or below the central line to accommodate the odd count.

deniers-30.name: Neuf de Deniers
deniers-30.Scene: The Six de Deniers shows six coins in a balanced arrangement, typically two columns of three. The six-coin card is among the more open pip compositions of the suit, the even number allowing a harmonious distribution without the density of the higher pip counts.

deniers-31.name: Dix de Deniers
deniers-31.Scene: The Cinq de Deniers shows five coins in a cross or quincunx arrangement — four at the corners and one at center. The five-coin card introduces the odd-number instability characteristic of pip fives, the central coin establishing a focal point around which the other four cluster.

deniers-32.name: Valet de Deniers
deniers-32.Scene: The Quatre de Deniers shows four coins in a square formation. The four-coin pip card is among the most stable of the suit — the four-fold arrangement provides symmetry in both axes, evoking solidity and foundation in the Italian pip tradition.

deniers-33.name: Cavalier de Deniers
deniers-33.Scene: The Trois de Deniers shows three coins in a triangular arrangement. The three-coin card introduces the minimal complexity of the Italian pip tradition — three is the first number that creates a spatial relationship beyond line or pair, the triangle of coins suggesting beginning organization.

deniers-34.name: Reine de Deniers
deniers-34.Scene: The Deux de Deniers shows two coins placed vertically or diagonally in simple correspondence. In the Italian pip tradition the two-coin card is sometimes embellished with a ribbon or decorative flourish connecting the coins, the pairing of two circular emblems being the suit's most elemental statement of duality.

deniers-35.name: Roi de Deniers
deniers-35.Scene: The As de Deniers shows a single large coin as the suit's foundational emblem. In the Italian-suited tradition the aces often carry additional decorative treatment — the single coin given an elaborate surround or ornamental context that marks it as the seed of the suit. The Paris anonymous ace of coins is the concentrated essence of the denier symbol.

suit-deniers.name: Deniers · Coins
suit-deniers.Scene: The suit of Deniers (Coins) in the Paris anonymous tarot uses the Italian-suited circular coin emblem with French court names: Roi, Reine, Cavalier, Valet. The pip cards follow standard Italian pip conventions with coin shapes in symmetrical distributions. This suit is part of the deck's Italian-suited structure within an otherwise distinctively French 17th-century production.

coupes-36.name: As de Coupes
coupes-36.Scene: The Roi de Coupes is the King of Cups in the Italian-suited Paris anonymous tarot. He appears enthroned with a chalice or cup as his suit emblem, the conventional seated king of the Italian pip-card tradition adapted to the cups suit. The cup king in the Paris anonymous deck follows the Marseille-derived iconography for the suit's highest court rank.

coupes-37.name: Deux de Coupes
coupes-37.Scene: The Reine de Coupes appears as the enthroned Queen of Cups, holding or displaying the chalice emblem in the conventional seated-queen posture. She is the feminine sovereign of the suit of feeling and inner life, the cups suit's highest feminine rank in the Paris anonymous tarot's Italian-suited court hierarchy.

coupes-38.name: Trois de Coupes
coupes-38.Scene: The Cavalier de Coupes is the mounted Knight of Cups, a horseman holding or presenting the cup emblem. The cavalier's mounted position marks his active engagement with the suit's emotional sphere, the cup borne forward on horseback as an act of pursuit or offering.

coupes-39.name: Quatre de Coupes
coupes-39.Scene: The Valet de Coupes is the standing Page of Cups, a young figure presenting or holding the chalice. The valet is the lowest court rank in the Italian-suited hierarchy, his standing posture and youth marking him as servant rather than sovereign of the suit.

coupes-40.name: Cinq de Coupes
coupes-40.Scene: The Dix de Coupes shows ten cups in the conventional Italian pip arrangement, the chalice or cup shapes distributed across the card in symmetrical formation. The ten-cup card marks the suit's fullness — all cups present, the emotional field complete.

coupes-41.name: Six de Coupes
coupes-41.Scene: The Neuf de Coupes shows nine cups in their conventional arrangement. The nine-cup card approaches the suit's fullness without completing it, a near-total field of chalices that suggests satisfaction held just short of its final form.

coupes-42.name: Sept de Coupes
coupes-42.Scene: The Huit de Coupes shows eight cups in a symmetrical pip arrangement. The even number allows a balanced two-column or two-row distribution of chalice emblems, the eight-cup card presenting the suit in its organized, stable mid-range.

coupes-43.name: Huit de Coupes
coupes-43.Scene: The Sept de Coupes shows seven cups distributed with the characteristic slight asymmetry of odd-number pip cards. Seven chalice shapes occupy the card's field, their odd count preventing perfect two-column symmetry and giving the card a quality of active emotional distribution.

coupes-44.name: Neuf de Coupes
coupes-44.Scene: The Six de Coupes shows six cups in a balanced two-column arrangement. The open, even distribution of the six-cup card gives the suit a quality of harmonious exchange — six chalices sharing the field with generous spacing between them.

coupes-45.name: Dix de Coupes
coupes-45.Scene: The Cinq de Coupes shows five cups in a cross or quincunx arrangement. The odd-number asymmetry of the five cups introduces an element of instability or loss into the suit's emotional field — something spilled or absent, the quincunx suggesting both fullness and gap.

coupes-46.name: Valet de Coupes
coupes-46.Scene: The Quatre de Coupes shows four cups in a square formation. The four-cup card is the suit's most stable pip composition — the square arrangement of four chalices suggesting emotional containment and security, feeling held in a firm four-fold structure.

coupes-47.name: Cavalier de Coupes
coupes-47.Scene: The Trois de Coupes shows three cups in a triangular arrangement. Three chalices in an implied triangle create the suit's first multi-point spatial relationship, the three cups suggesting a community or shared emotional ground rather than mere pairing.

coupes-48.name: Reine de Coupes
coupes-48.Scene: The Deux de Coupes shows two cups placed in vertical or diagonal correspondence. The two-cup card is the suit's primal emotional dyad — two chalices facing or echoing each other, the minimal expression of emotional exchange and reciprocity.

coupes-49.name: Roi de Coupes
coupes-49.Scene: The As de Coupes shows a single large chalice as the suit's foundational emblem. In the Italian pip tradition the cup ace is often the most ornate of the suit's pip cards, the single chalice given decorative treatment that marks it as the undivided potential of the emotional realm.

suit-coupes.name: Coupes · Cups
suit-coupes.Scene: The suit of Coupes (Cups) in the Paris anonymous tarot uses the Italian-suited chalice emblem with French court names: Roi, Reine, Cavalier, Valet. The pip cards follow standard Italian conventions with cup shapes in symmetrical distributions. Within a deck famous for its unusual trumps, the cups suit carries the more conventional iconography of the Italian pip tradition.

batons-50.name: As de Bâtons
batons-50.Scene: The Roi de Bâtons is the King of Batons in the Italian-suited Paris anonymous tarot. He appears enthroned holding the baton or staff as his suit emblem, the king of wands in the Italian pip tradition adapted to the French court context. The baton king's authority is associated with fire and creative energy.

batons-51.name: Deux de Bâtons
batons-51.Scene: The Reine de Bâtons appears as the enthroned Queen of Batons, holding or displaying the staff emblem in the conventional seated-queen posture. She is the feminine sovereign of the suit of fire and creative enterprise in the Paris anonymous tarot's Italian-suited court hierarchy.

batons-52.name: Trois de Bâtons
batons-52.Scene: The Cavalier de Bâtons is the mounted Knight of Batons, a horseman holding or brandishing the staff. The mounted knight of the baton suit in the Italian pip tradition embodies fiery forward momentum — the wand-bearer whose charge carries creative force into active expression.

batons-53.name: Quatre de Bâtons
batons-53.Scene: The Valet de Bâtons is the standing Page of Batons, a young figure holding or presenting the staff. The valet of the baton suit is the suit's most youthful and immediate expression — a page who carries the wand's creative potential without yet having directed it toward a specific enterprise.

batons-54.name: Cinq de Bâtons
batons-54.Scene: The Dix de Bâtons shows ten staff shapes in the dense interlocking arrangement typical of the baton suit's highest pip card. In the Italian-suited convention the ten batons are crowded and overlapping, the suit's energy accumulated to a point of burdensome fullness. The ten-baton card is the most heavily loaded of the suit's pip compositions.

batons-55.name: Six de Bâtons
batons-55.Scene: The Neuf de Bâtons shows nine staff shapes approaching the density of the ten. The nine batons carry the suit near its maximum load without yet completing it, an arrangement that suggests energy still active and unresolved rather than simply accumulated.

batons-56.name: Sept de Bâtons
batons-56.Scene: The Huit de Bâtons shows eight staff shapes in a symmetrical crossing arrangement. The even number allows the batons to form a geometric pattern, the eight staves crossing in pairs or groups to create an organized visual field that suggests the suit's energy channeled rather than merely accumulated.

batons-57.name: Huit de Bâtons
batons-57.Scene: The Sept de Bâtons shows seven staff shapes in a slightly asymmetric arrangement, the odd number preventing perfect bilateral symmetry. The seven batons in contest or in slight imbalance suggest an active, contested moment within the suit's energetic field.

batons-58.name: Neuf de Bâtons
batons-58.Scene: The Six de Bâtons shows six staff shapes in a balanced arrangement, the even distribution of the baton suit at its mid-range. Six staves crossed or arranged in pairs create a composition that suggests equilibrium rather than contest within the suit's domain of creative energy.

batons-59.name: Dix de Bâtons
batons-59.Scene: The Cinq de Bâtons shows five staff shapes with the characteristic tension of the suit's odd-number pip cards. Five batons in a contest arrangement suggest active encounter — the suit's energy at a point of competitive engagement, the five staves implied in motion against each other.

batons-60.name: Valet de Bâtons
batons-60.Scene: The Quatre de Bâtons shows four staff shapes in a square or cross formation. The four-baton card is among the most stable of the suit's pip compositions — four staves at four corners suggest the foundation of creative enterprise, a structure that supports further building.

batons-61.name: Cavalier de Bâtons
batons-61.Scene: The Trois de Bâtons shows three staff shapes in a triangular arrangement. The three batons suggest creative momentum — three staves in relation rather than mere pairing, the triangle of force that marks the beginning of organized enterprise.

batons-62.name: Reine de Bâtons
batons-62.Scene: The Deux de Bâtons shows two staff shapes in crossing or parallel correspondence. The two batons are the suit's primal pairing — two wands in initial relation, the minimal expression of creative force meeting itself or its complement.

batons-63.name: Roi de Bâtons
batons-63.Scene: The As de Bâtons shows a single large staff as the suit's foundational emblem. In the Italian pip tradition the baton ace is typically the most unadorned and direct expression of the suit — a single wand or staff, the creative force undivided.

suit-batons.name: Bâtons · Batons
suit-batons.Scene: The suit of Bâtons (Batons) in the Paris anonymous tarot uses the Italian-suited staff or wand emblem with French court names: Roi, Reine, Cavalier, Valet. The pip cards follow standard Italian conventions with stave shapes in crossing and symmetrical arrangements. Within a deck famous for its unusual trumps, the batons suit carries the more conventional iconography of the Italian pip tradition.

epees-64.name: As de Épées
epees-64.Scene: The Roi d'Épées is the King of Swords in the Italian-suited Paris anonymous tarot. He appears enthroned with a long sword as his suit emblem, the king of blades in the Italian pip tradition. The sword king's authority is associated with intellect, judgment, and the power of decisive action.

epees-65.name: Deux de Épées
epees-65.Scene: The Reine d'Épées appears as the enthroned Queen of Swords, holding or displaying the sword emblem in the conventional seated-queen posture. She is the feminine sovereign of the suit of thought and discernment in the Paris anonymous tarot's Italian-suited court hierarchy.

epees-66.name: Trois de Épées
epees-66.Scene: The Cavalier d'Épées is the mounted Knight of Swords, a horseman charging with sword raised or extended. The sword knight's mounted posture embodies the suit's decisive, cutting energy in motion — the blade carried forward on horseback as an act of swift judgment or attack.

epees-67.name: Quatre de Épées
epees-67.Scene: The Valet d'Épées is the standing Page of Swords, a young figure holding or presenting the sword. The valet of the sword suit is the suit's youthful bearer — a page who carries the blade's potential for precision and challenge without yet having exercised it in full.

epees-68.name: Cinq de Épées
epees-68.Scene: The Dix d'Épées shows ten sword shapes in the conventional Italian pip arrangement. In the Italian-suited tradition the ten of swords is among the densest pip compositions, the ten blades interlocking or crossing in a field that suggests the suit's accumulated cutting force at its maximum.

epees-69.name: Six de Épées
epees-69.Scene: The Neuf d'Épées shows nine sword shapes approaching the density of the ten. The nine blades fill the card's field without yet reaching the ten's completeness, the suit's accumulated sharpness near its peak.

epees-70.name: Sept de Épées
epees-70.Scene: The Huit d'Épées shows eight sword shapes in a symmetrical arrangement. The even number allows the eight blades to form balanced crossing patterns, the suit's energy organized through geometric symmetry in the Italian pip convention.

epees-71.name: Huit de Épées
epees-71.Scene: The Sept d'Épées shows seven sword shapes in a slightly asymmetric arrangement. Seven blades resist perfect bilateral symmetry, giving the card an active, slightly off-balance quality that suggests contest or alert readiness within the suit's intellectual domain.

epees-72.name: Neuf de Épées
epees-72.Scene: The Six d'Épées shows six sword shapes in a balanced arrangement of the Italian pip convention. The six blades are distributed in pairs or columns, the even number allowing a harmonious and readable composition within the suit's field of cutting clarity.

epees-73.name: Dix de Épées
epees-73.Scene: The Cinq d'Épées shows five sword shapes with the characteristic asymmetry of odd-number pip cards. Five blades arranged with a central dominant sword suggest contested division — the suit's energy at a point of active conflict rather than settled arrangement.

epees-74.name: Valet de Épées
epees-74.Scene: The Quatre d'Épées shows four sword shapes in a square or cross formation. The four-sword card is among the more stable pip compositions of the suit — four blades at four points suggest rest or structured positioning, the suit's energy held in a firm four-fold arrangement.

epees-75.name: Cavalier de Épées
epees-75.Scene: The Trois d'Épées shows three sword shapes crossing at or near the card's center. Three blades in crossing or triangular arrangement create the suit's minimal field of intersection — three points of sharpness in relation, the first multi-point crossing of the Italian sword pip.

epees-76.name: Reine de Épées
epees-76.Scene: The Deux d'Épées shows two sword shapes crossed in X formation. The two blades in crossing are the suit's primal opposition — the simplest visible expression of the conflict, judgment, and discernment that define the sword suit in the Italian pip tradition.

epees-77.name: Roi de Épées
epees-77.Scene: The As d'Épées shows a single large sword as the suit's foundational emblem. In the Italian pip tradition the sword ace is typically bold and heraldic, the single blade — often shown with a crown or decorative surround — as the undivided potential of the suit's cutting clarity.

suit-epees.name: Épées · Swords
suit-epees.Scene: The suit of Épées (Swords) in the Paris anonymous tarot uses the Italian-suited long sword emblem with French court names: Roi, Reine, Cavalier, Valet. The pip cards follow standard Italian conventions with blade shapes in crossing and symmetrical arrangements. The sword suit's Italian-tradition iconography carries the conventional pip vocabulary within a deck whose trumps are among the most unusual in the Marseille tradition.

trump-mat.name: Le Mat (The Fool)
trump-mat.Scene: Le Mat is the unnumbered Fool of the Paris anonymous deck — a vagabond or wandering figure broadly comparable to the Marseille Fool with his bundle and torn clothes. The Paris Fool occupies the conventional social position of the outcast without rank who travels outside the sequence of numbered trumps, his freedom from number signaling his exemption from the structured world the other cards represent.

axis-atouts.name: Les Atouts (22 Trumps)
axis-atouts.Scene: A navigational axis grouping all twenty-two Paris anonymous trump cards together. Among the most celebrated departures from the Marseille tradition: a goose-drawn chariot with child rider at VII, a Janus-faced Justice at VIII, a scholar measuring the heavens for the Star, a romantic serenade for the Moon, and a monkey vanity scene for the Sun. The Paris anonymous tarot is one of the earliest and most distinctive surviving French tarots.
